newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuelan Central Bank warns of rising inflation.
newsitem.headline: Venezuelan Central Bank warns of rising inflation.

text.p: Venezuelan inflation at the end of last year was higher than previously targeted, Central Bank president Antonio Casas Gonzalez said, and without fiscal discipline could rise again this year.
"Threats to longed-for price stability still exist and in some respects are increasing," Casas said in statement released on Thursday by the Central Bank.
"The oil bonanza ... ought not be an excuse for undisciplined public spending which would soon produce a rise in inflation," he said.

Casas's remarks came only two days after March figures showed inflation had slowed to 1.6 percent -- versus February's 2.3 percent rate -- the lowest inflation rate in five years and well below market expectations of around 2.5 percent.

Despite the drop, many analysts fear Venezuela will overshoot its ambitious 30-35 percent inflation target for the year due to a recent 70 percent public sector pay rise and a severance pay reform deal reached in March.

Casas welcomed the ground-breaking severance pay reform agreement, but cautioned that: "all institutions and sectors of Venezuelan society should re-double their efforts to fight inflation." Casas re-affirmed the Central Bank's commitment to do this, but "within a context of coordinated stabilization efforts."

The planned creation of a Macroeconomic Stabilization Fund that would squirrel away oil price windfalls "is a clear sign of the Government's, Congress's and the public's desire to act with prudence when there's is a passing bonanza," he said.

But while reviewing the second half of 1996 Casas said that although inflation had tended down to 25.3 percent, versus 62.3 percent in the first half, the fall had not been as great as expected due to increased government spending on the back of higher than expected oil revenues.
Inflation topped 103 percent in 1996, but has tended downwards since May when Venezuela began a tough series of IMF- sponsored reforms.
Inflation for the first quarter of this year was 6.6 percent, but is expected to rise when backdated severance pay due under the recent reform agreement, as well as public sector pay rises, are paid.
